Fix a coordinate orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ for the mirror convention. Let $K$ and $J$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere. Choose this standard map once in the standard two-ball model so that it commutes with $r$ and an orientation-preserving half-turn interchanging the two balls preserves the joining convention. The **standard unknot** is the oriented unit circle in a fixed coordinate two-plane of $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$. A knot is **nontrivial** if it is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ to the standard unknot. A nontrivial knot is **prime** if it has no connected-sum presentation whose two summand knots are both nontrivial.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

1. **Compact main case.** Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold, possibly with boundary, let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $F:M\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings that is constant near the ends of $I$, and let $W$ be an open neighbourhood of $F(M\times I)$ in $N$. Then there is an ambient isotopy $H:N\times I\to N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, every $H_t$ a diffeomorphism, $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ for all $t\in I$, $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ outside $W$ for every $t$, and $H_t$ stationary near the ends; if $F$ is constant near the ends with parameter $\varepsilon$, then $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ for $t\le\varepsilon/2$ and $H_t=H_1$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon/2$.
2. **Relative form.** Let $N$ be boundaryless, $U\subseteq N$ open, $A\subseteq U$ compact, and let $F:U\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings whose track image is open in $N\times I$. Then there is a compactly supported ambient isotopy $H$ of $N$ with $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$.
3. **Boundary stratum.** If $N$ has boundary and $F(M\times I)\subseteq\partial N$, then the ambient isotopy of clause 1 can be chosen with every $H_t$ carrying $\partial N$ onto itself; if $F(M\times I)\subseteq N\setminus\partial N$, it can be chosen compactly supported in $N\setminus\partial N$.
4. **General isotopies.** For the same compact source (possibly with boundary) and boundaryless target as in clause 1, every smooth isotopy extends with support in a compact subset of any prescribed neighbourhood $W$ of $F(M\times I)$. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Put $\theta_t=(1-t)\theta_0$ and define $H_t(s)=(\cos\theta_t e^{2\pi i\varepsilon s},\sin\theta_t e^{2\pi i q s})$. Each $H_t$ lies in $S^3$; its first coordinate is an injective circle parameterization because $|\varepsilon|=1$ and $\cos\theta_t>0$, and the family is smooth including $t=1$. It begins with the given orientation and ends at the core circle with orientation sign $\varepsilon$.

If $q=\varepsilon\in\{1,-1\}$, the path $(z_1,z_2)\mapsto(\cos t\,z_1+\sin t\,z_2,-\sin t\,z_1+\cos t\,z_2)$, $0\le t\le\pi/2$, lies in $SO(4)$ and isotopes the identity to $(z_1,z_2)\mapsto(z_2,-z_1)$. The image of the curve is $(\sin\theta_0 e^{2\pi i\varepsilon s},-r e^{2\pi i p s})$. Let $\eta_0\in(0,\pi/2)$ satisfy $\cos\eta_0=\sin\theta_0$ and $\sin\eta_0=r$, put $\eta_t=(1-t)\eta_0$, and use $H_t(s)=(\cos\eta_t e^{2\pi i\varepsilon s},-\sin\eta_t e^{2\pi i p s})$. Its first coordinate has winding $\varepsilon=\pm1$, so the family is a smooth isotopy through embeddings to the core with orientation sign $\varepsilon$. The initial coordinate rotation also preserves the knot orientation because it is an ambient isotopy.

By [F3], each smooth isotopy of the compact embedded circle constructed above extends to an ambient isotopy of $S^3$. Its terminal core is the standard unknot, with orientation sign $\varepsilon$. If $\varepsilon=-1$, write $z_j=x_j+i y_j$ and define $R_\tau(x_1,y_1,x_2,y_2)=(x_1,y_1\cos\tau+y_2\sin\tau,x_2,-y_1\sin\tau+y_2\cos\tau)$. This is a rotation in the $(y_1,y_2)$-plane, so $R_\tau$ is an orientation-preserving isometry of $S^3$ from the identity to $R_\pi(z_1,z_2)=(\overline z_1,\overline z_2)$. On the core, $R_\pi(e^{2\pi i s},0)=(e^{-2\pi i s},0)$, so this ambient isotopy reverses its orientation. In either sign case the original oriented curve is ambient isotopic to the standard oriented unknot.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere $S^3$. A **Seifert surface** for $K$ is a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface $F\subset S^3$ with boundary set equal to $K$. Orient each boundary component so that an outward-pointing conormal in $F$, followed by a positive boundary tangent, is a positive basis of $TF$; the oriented boundary of $F$ must agree with the given orientation of $K$. For such a surface, its genus $g(F)$ is the unique nonnegative integer satisfying $\chi(F)=2-2g(F)-b$, where $b$ is the number of boundary components; here $b=1$, so $\chi(F)=1-2g(F)$. The compact-surface normal-form result supplies this integer under the stated choice axiom.

derivations.claim: Use the solid-torus side with core the first-coordinate circle, so the second coordinate is the meridional disk coordinate. At longitudinal angle $u\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ in the first coordinate, the knot meets this disk at the $p$ points with second-coordinate angles $2\pi q(u+k)/p$, $k=0,\ldots,p-1$. Place these points at the vertices of a regular $p$-gon. A counterclockwise rotation by $2\pi/p$, tapered to fix the disk boundary, carries each point to the next and crosses consecutive points once in the order $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_{p-1}$; each $\sigma_i$ is the positive half twist of adjacent points. Thus one such increment is the braid block $\delta=\sigma_1\cdots\sigma_{p-1}$, and the rotation through $2\pi q/p$ gives $\delta^q$. The lifted curve has winding vector $(p,q)$ in the fixed Heegaard-torus coordinates, exactly the parameterization in [F1]. The braid block permutes the points by a $p$-cycle, so its $q$th power has one cycle because $\gcd(p,q)=1$.

At each positive crossing replace the crossing by the orientation-compatible smoothing and then attach one half-twisted rectangle in the original crossing ball; this is the oriented braid Seifert-surface construction. It gives $p$ disks joined by $q(p-1)$ positively half-twisted bands, one for each crossing. The first block has one band between each adjacent pair of disks, so its incidence graph is a path; attaching bands along a tree joins the disks to a disk. Each of the remaining $q-1$ blocks has $p-1$ bands.

Add the remaining blocks in order, and within each block add the bands in the order $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_{p-1}$. For each added band, a small ball containing it and the corresponding band from the preceding block can be chosen disjoint from the other crossing balls after sliding their strand rectangles along the Seifert disks. The two bands are positive half twists on the same adjacent pair; their union with the two intervening disk strips is an annulus whose boundary components have linking number $+1$, hence a positive Hopf band. The old band meets the already-built surface in a square, the new annulus lies on the opposite side of that square, and the orientations agree because both bands come from positive crossings. Thus each added band is exactly a plumbing along a square as defined in the Statement. Repeating this for all $(q-1)(p-1)$ later bands gives the stated grid of positive Hopf plumbings.

A plumbing replaces the old square and the Hopf annulus by their union, so inclusion-exclusion for Euler characteristic gives $\chi(F_{p,q})=\chi(F_{p,q}^{\mathrm{old}})+0-1=\chi(F_{p,q}^{\mathrm{old}})-1$. Starting from the disk in step 2.1, after $(p-1)(q-1)$ plumbings the surface is connected and has $\chi(F_{p,q})=1-(p-1)(q-1)$.

The boundary of the constructed surface is the closure of the braid in step 1.1. Its permutation has one cycle, so the boundary has one component; the construction is connected and oriented at every band attachment. It is therefore a Seifert surface for $T(p,q)$ in the sense of [F2].
Since $(p-1)(q-1)$ is even, the one-boundary-component identity $\chi(F)=1-2g(F)$ and step 4.1 give $g(F_{p,q})=(p-1)(q-1)/2$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

derivations.claim: The primitive slope $p\alpha+q\beta$ is essential on the Heegaard torus. Removing a small annular neighborhood of $K$ from that torus leaves a closed annulus $A$. On either side, removing the corresponding half of the tube from a solid torus only removes a boundary collar, so the two pieces retract to solid tori $W_x,W_y$ and their overlap retracts to $A$. Thicken the pieces by half-collars to obtain path-connected open sets covering $E_K$ whose intersection retracts to $A$. The core of $A$ winds $p$ times around the core generator $x$ on one side and $q$ times around $y$ on the other. Full AC [A1] supplies the countable-choice hypothesis of [F2] by [L1].

The action $\rho_t$ is isometric for the round metric. Its generic orbits have slope $(p,q)$ and trivial stabilizer because $\gcd(p,q)=1$; hence the metric tube chosen in the Statement is invariant. The coordinate circles $z_1=0$ and $z_2=0$ have stabilizer orders $|q|$ and $|p|$ respectively. The orbit space is a sphere: on each torus $|z_1|=r$ with $0<r<1$, quotienting by the primitive circle orbit leaves a circle, and the two end circles collapse to the two coordinate-orbit points. Removing the invariant tube removes a disk from the orbit sphere, so the exterior is fibered over a disk with the stated multiplicities. Multiplicity one is the regular local model; multiplicity greater than one is exceptional.

The three fundamental groups in this cover are $\pi_1(W_x)=\langle x\rangle\cong\mathbb Z$, $\pi_1(W_y)=\langle y\rangle\cong\mathbb Z$, and $\pi_1(A)=\langle a\rangle\cong\mathbb Z$, with inclusion maps $a\mapsto x^p$ and $a\mapsto y^q$. By [F4], $\pi_1(E_K)$ is their pushout. A group receiving maps from the two cyclic factors is determined by images of $x,y$; the maps agree on the intersection exactly when $x^p=y^q$. Hence the pushout has presentation $\langle x,y\mid x^p=y^q\rangle$.

A regular orbit parallel to $K$ represents the annulus core $x^p=y^q=h$. This element commutes with $x$ because it is $x^p$, and commutes with $y$ because it is $y^q$; as $x,y$ generate the group from step 2.1, $h$ is central.

Choose integers $c,d$ with $pd-qc=1$ and let $L=c\alpha+d\beta$ be the corresponding simple curve on the Heegaard torus; its algebraic intersection with $K$ is one. At the intersection, the boundary $m$ of a small normal disk splits into arcs $\gamma_x,\gamma_y$ on the two solid-torus sides, while $L$ splits into its crossing arc and complementary arc $L_1$. Inserting $L_1L_1^{-1}$ into $m=\gamma_x\gamma_y$ gives $m=(\gamma_xL_1)(L_1^{-1}\gamma_y)$. The first factor winds $c$ times around the $x$ core and the second winds $-d$ times around the $y$ core, hence $m=x^c y^{-d}$. Its abelianization under $x\mapsto q$, $y\mapsto p$ is $cq-dp=-1$, so it is opposite the positive normal-disk meridian, whose class is the positive generator by [F3]. Thus $\mu=m^{-1}=y^d x^{-c}$. Setting $\alpha=d$ and $\beta=-c$ gives $p\alpha+q\beta=1$ and the stated word; another Bezout solution changes the exponents by $(qk,-pk)$, so the word is unchanged because $y^{qk}=h^k=x^{pk}$ and $h$ is central.

Abelianizing the presentation in step 2.1 gives the relation $p[x]=q[y]$. The map $x\mapsto q$, $y\mapsto p$ is surjective because $\gcd(p,q)=1$, and its kernel in $\mathbb Z^2$ is generated by $(p,-q)$, exactly the relation vector; hence it identifies this quotient with $\mathbb Z$. Step 3.2 sends the positive meridian to $1$, so by [F3] it is the positive generator of $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$. Thus $[h]=p[x]=pq[\mu]$. The regular orbit $h$ is a degree-one parallel of $K$ on $\partial E_K$, and $\mu$ has degree zero there, so $\lambda=h\mu^{-pq}$ has degree one and zero image in $H_1(E_K)$. Uniqueness in [F3] identifies it with the preferred longitude; [F3] also proves that $[\mu],[\lambda]$ form a basis of $H_1(\partial E_K;\mathbb Z)$, so each is primitive.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $p,q$ be coprime nonzero integers, let $K=T(p,q)$ be the oriented primitive slope curve in the standard Heegaard torus, and let $\rho_t(z_1,z_2)=(e^{2\pi i p t}z_1,e^{2\pi i q t}z_2)$ be the weighted circle action on the unit $S^3\subset\mathbb C^2$. Choose $N(K)$ to be a sufficiently small closed metric tube around the orbit $K$ for the round metric; this tube is invariant because $\rho_t$ is isometric and preserves $K$. Set $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$. Let $x$ and $y$ be based generators of the fundamental groups of the two solid-torus pieces obtained by cutting $E_K$ along the annulus left on the Heegaard torus, oriented so that the annulus core maps to $x^p$ and $y^q$. Then

$$\pi_1(E_K)=\langle x,y\mid x^p=y^q\rangle.$$

The common element $h=x^p=y^q$ is central and represents a regular fiber of a Seifert fibration of $E_K$ over a disk. The fibration has two distinguished core fibers of multiplicities $|p|$ and $|q|$; a fiber of multiplicity one is regular, and a fiber of multiplicity greater than one is exceptional. Thus there are exactly two exceptional fibers when $|p|,|q|>1$, and one is regular when one absolute parameter is $1$.

For any integers $\alpha,\beta$ with $p\alpha+q\beta=1$, compatible based paths identify the positive normal-disk meridian and preferred longitude in the peripheral system as

$$\mu=y^\alpha x^\beta,\qquad \lambda=h\mu^{-pq}.$$

Here the positive meridian is the oriented boundary of a normal disk, and the preferred longitude has degree one around $K$ and maps to zero in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$. Their homology classes form a basis of $H_1(\partial E_K;\mathbb Z)$, so both classes are primitive.

Assume countable choice. Let $K:S^1	o S^3$ be a smooth oriented embedding and write its quotient normal bundle as $
u_K=K^*TS^3/dK(TS^1)$. Choose an orientation-preserving trivialization $
u_K\cong S^1	imes\mathbb R^2$ and a tubular map $\Phi:\Omega	o S^3$, meaning a smooth embedding from an open neighbourhood $\Omega\subseteq
u_K$ of the zero section onto an open neighbourhood of $K(S^1)$ with $\Phi(s,0)=K(s)$, such that in these product coordinates $\Omega$ contains $S^1	imes D^2_{2\epsilon}$ for some $\epsilon>0$. Here $D^2_r=\{z\in\mathbb R^2:\|z\|\le r\}$ uses the product Euclidean norm induced by the chosen trivialization. Set $N(K)=\Phi(S^1	imes D^2_\epsilon)$, $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$, $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ be inclusion, $p:T_K	o S^1$ the product projection, and $\mu$ the positive boundary of a normal disk, using the normal-plane orientation determined by the orientations of $K$ and $S^3$. A class is primitive if it is not $m$ times another class for any integer $|m|>1$. Then $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ is generated by $[\mu]$. The kernel of $i_*:H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)	o H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ is a primitive rank-one direct summand generated by a unique class $[\lambda]$ with $p_*[\lambda]=1\in H_1(S^1;\mathbb Z)$. It has a simple closed representative, is the preferred longitude, and $([\mu],[\lambda])$ is a basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$.

Assume countable choice. For every smooth oriented knot $K$ in $S^3$, there are an oriented normal-bundle trivialization, a tubular map $\Phi$ defined on an open neighbourhood containing $S^1\times D^2_{2\epsilon}$ for some $\epsilon>0$, and a closed tubular neighbourhood $N(K)=\Phi(S^1\times D^2_\epsilon)$. This $N(K)$ is diffeomorphic to $S^1\times D^2$, its boundary $T_K$ is diffeomorphic to $S^1\times S^1$, and its exterior $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ is a compact smooth oriented three-manifold with boundary $T_K$. The open complement $S^3\setminus K$ strongly deformation retracts onto $E_K$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$ be an
oriented link with $r\ge1$ components and complement $X_L$,
([[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]]), and let
$$\varphi:H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow\mathbb Z$$
be the **total linking homomorphism**, defined as the composite
$$H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow[\ \sim\ ]{\mathrm{Alex}}\widetilde H^1(L;\mathbb Z)\cong\bigoplus_{i=1}^rH^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow{\text{sum}}\mathbb Z,$$
where the first arrow is Alexander duality
([[thm-alexander-duality-for-compact-locally-contractible-subsets-of-a-sphere]]),
each $H^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ is the orientation-induced
identification, and the last map sums the $r$ coordinates. By
[[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization]] the map $\varphi$
may again be written $\pi_1(X_L)\to H_1(X_L)\xrightarrow{\varphi}\mathbb Z$; we
denote both composites by $\varphi$ and set $K:=\ker\varphi$.

The **one-variable Alexander module** of $L$ is
$$A_L:=H_1(\widetilde{X_L};\mathbb Z),$$
the first singular homology of the connected infinite cyclic cover
$p:\widetilde{X_L}\to X_L$ classified by $K$
([[thm-classification-of-connected-covering-spaces]],
[[lem-subgroup-quotient-of-universal-cover]],
[[def-covering-map-and-evenly-covered-neighbourhoods]]), equipped with its
structure of module over $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$
([[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]]) in which $t$ acts by the deck
transformation corresponding to the positive generator of
$\operatorname{Deck}(\widetilde{X_L}/X_L)\cong\mathbb Z$.

**Caveats.** The cover is the one classified by $K=\ker\varphi$; since $K$ is
normal the cover is regular and its deck group is
$\pi_1(X_L)/K\cong\mathbb Z$
([[def-regular-covering]], [[thm-regular-covering-characterizations]], [[cor-deck-group-of-a-regular-covering]],
[[def-deck-transformation-and-deck-group]]). The module $A_L$ is ordinary
integral homology of the cover, with the deck action as its module structure;
no twisting by a representation of the link group is used. The total linking
homomorphism satisfies $\varphi(\mu_i)=1$ for a meridian $\mu_i$ of any one
component, so $r\ge1$ is needed for $\varphi$ to be interesting and $A_L$
depends on the orientations of all components through this map.

For every CW complex $X$, abelian group $G$, and $n\geq0$, the cellular complex has an
isomorphism $H_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(X;G)\cong H_n(X;G)$, natural with respect to
cellular maps.

For every path-connected topological space $X$ and $x_0\in X$, the Hurewicz map
$$h:\pi_1(X,x_0)\longrightarrow H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$$
is surjective and has kernel $[\pi_1(X,x_0),\pi_1(X,x_0)]$. Hence it induces a natural isomorphism
$$\pi_1(X,x_0)^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong H_1(X;\mathbb Z).$$
The proof is choice-free and requires no CW, separation, local path-connectivity or local simple-connectivity assumption.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring ([[def-commutative-ring]]) and let $M$ be a
finitely presented $R$-module ([[def-finitely-presented-module-and-algebra]]),
so that there are $m,n\in\mathbb N$ and a presentation

$$R^m\xrightarrow{\ A\ }R^n\xrightarrow{\ \beta\ }M\longrightarrow0 .$$

Fix the standard bases $e_1,\dots,e_m$ of $R^m$ and $f_1,\dots,f_n$ of $R^n$
([[def-finitely-presented-module-and-algebra]]) and let $A=(a_{ij})$ be the
$n\times m$ matrix of the $R$-linear map $\alpha$ with respect to them: the
$j$-th column of $A$ is the coordinate vector of $\alpha(e_j)$, so
$\alpha(e_j)=\sum_{i=1}^n a_{ij}f_i$. Such a matrix is called a **presentation
matrix** of $M$ (for the chosen presentation). A **minor** of $A$ of size
$r\times r$ is the determinant $\det(a_{i_sj_t})_{s,t=1}^r$
([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]) of the square submatrix obtained by
choosing rows $i_1<\dots<i_r$ and columns $j_1<\dots<j_r$; determinants of
$1\times1$ and $0\times0$ submatrices are allowed, with the empty determinant
equal to $1$.

For $k\ge0$ the **$k$-th elementary ideal** $E_k(M)$ of the presented module $M$
is the ideal of $R$ generated by the determinants of **all**
$(n-k)\times(n-k)$ minors of $A$ ([[def-generated-and-principal-ideals]],
[[def-left-right-and-two-sided-ideal]]): if $n-k>n$ or $n-k>m$ there is no such
minor, and the ideal generated by the empty set is $0$. In particular no minor
is nonzero-by-convention: the conventions are
$$E_k(M)=R\quad\text{for }k\ge n,\qquad E_k(M)=0\quad\text{for }k<n-m .$$
For $0\le k\le\min(n,m)$ the ideal $E_k(M)$ is the ideal generated by the
$(n-k)\times(n-k)$ minors; e.g. $E_1(M)$ is generated by the
$(n-1)\times(n-1)$ minors of $A$, and $E_n(M)=R$ because the $0\times0$ minor
is $1$. This is the $k$-th **Fitting ideal** $\operatorname{Fit}_k(M)$ of the
Stacks Project (Tag 07Z6, Lemma 15.8.2 and Definition 15.8.3), which is
indexed by the size $n-k$ of the complementary minors; the two conventions
$0=E_{-1}\subset E_0\subset\cdots$ agree on the range $0\le k\le\min(n,m)$.

**Caveats.** (i) The notation $E_k(M)$ suppresses the chosen presentation; the
ideal defined here is a priori attached to the presentation and it is the
content of [[lem-elementary-ideals-are-independent-of-the-presentation]] that
it is in fact an invariant of $M$. (ii) The conventions in the degenerate
ranges are conventions, not theorems; they are the ones compatible with the
Stacks numbering and with independence of the presentation.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, so that the Alexander module $A_L$ of an oriented
nonempty link $L$ is defined and finitely presented over
$\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$
([[def-one-variable-alexander-module-of-an-oriented-link]],
[[lem-the-alexander-module-of-a-link-complement-is-finitely-presented]]). Let
$r$ be the number of components of $L$. Define the **one-variable Alexander
polynomial** $\Delta_L(t)\in\Lambda$ to be a greatest common divisor of the zeroth
elementary ideal $E_0(A_L)$
([[def-elementary-ideals-of-a-finitely-presented-module]]), i.e. a generator of
the smallest principal ideal of $\Lambda$ containing $E_0(A_L)$
([[lem-the-laurent-polynomial-ring-is-noetherian-and-a-unique-factorisation-domain]],
[[def-unique-factorisation-domain]]); it is well defined up to multiplication
by a unit $\pm t^k$ of $\Lambda$
([[lem-units-and-powers-of-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]]). The **Alexander
invariant** is the normalisation
$$D_L(t):=\begin{cases}\Delta_L(t),&r>1,\\[2pt] \dfrac{\Delta_L(t)}{1-t},&r=1,\end{cases}$$
understood for a knot as an element of the fraction field of $\Lambda$ when
$(1-t)\nmid\Delta_L(t)$; for the integer-valued link formulas of this page the
distinction matters and is stated with each use.

**Caveats.** The ideal $E_0(A_L)$ is a well-defined invariant of $L$ because
$A_L$ is finitely presented and elementary ideals are independent of the
presentation
([[lem-elementary-ideals-are-independent-of-the-presentation]]); a greatest
common divisor in a unique factorisation domain is well defined up to units, and
the units of $\Lambda$ are $\pm t^k$. For every link the absolute one-variable Alexander module admits a square
presentation, so $E_0(A_L)$ is principal, generated by its determinant (the
standard link fact recorded in [F3]). For a knot ($r=1$), every gcd
representative satisfies $\Delta_L(1)=\pm1$. These standard presentation and
normalisation facts are recorded here; the gcd definition itself uses only
finite presentability and unique factorisation.

The Laurent polynomial ring $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$ of
[[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]] is Noetherian, hence every ideal of
$\Lambda$ is finitely generated, and $\Lambda$ is a unique factorisation
domain; its units are $\pm t^k$, $k\in\mathbb Z$, and $t$ is prime in $\mathbb Z[t]$ but becomes a unit in $\Lambda$.

derivations.claim: Abelianizing the presentation in [F1] gives the relation $p[x]=q[y]$. The map $\phi(x)=q$, $\phi(y)=p$ is onto because $\gcd(p,q)=1$; its kernel in $\mathbb Z^2$ is generated by $(p,-q)$, exactly the abelianized relation vector, so the abelianization is $\mathbb Z$. The meridian in [F1] maps to $p\alpha+q\beta=1$, so the epimorphism $\phi$ in the Statement is precisely the positive total-linking homomorphism that classifies the cover in [F4].

For every integer $n$, $(z^n-1)/(z-1)$ is a finite Laurent sum; for $n<0$ it equals $-(z^{-1}+\cdots+z^n)$. In the lifted attaching word, a positive edge contributes the current deck translate and a negative edge contributes the negative of the preceding translate. The $x^p$ block therefore contributes $(x^p-1)/(x-1)$ to the $x$-edge coordinate. The following $y^{-q}$ block starts after the $x^p$ translate and contributes $x^p(y^{-q}-1)/(y-1)$ to the $y$-edge coordinate. These are the complete signed edge contributions of the two-cell in $\widetilde P_\phi$.

The cyclic cover in the Statement has cellular chain groups $C_2=\Lambda$, $C_1=\Lambda^2$, $C_0=\Lambda$. Its first boundary is $d_1=(t^q-1,\ t^p-1)$ because lifted $x$- and $y$-edges end $q$ and $p$ deck steps from their starts. Evaluating the two edge contributions in step 1.2 at $x=t^q$, $y=t^p$ gives the second boundary column; the $y$-coordinate is $t^{pq}(t^{-pq}-1)/(t^p-1)=-(t^{pq}-1)/(t^p-1)$:
$$d_2(1)=\left(\frac{t^{pq}-1}{t^q-1},\ -\frac{t^{pq}-1}{t^p-1}\right)^T.$$
This is the cellular boundary of the lifted two-cell.

In $\Lambda$, $\gcd(t^p-1,t^q-1)\doteq t-1$: for positive exponents the Euclidean algorithm gives this because $\gcd(|p|,|q|)=1$, and negative exponents differ from the positive ones by units. Hence $a=(t^q-1)/(t-1)$ and $b=(t^p-1)/(t-1)$ are coprime. The kernel of $d_1$ is the free rank-one submodule generated by $(b,-a)^T$: if $au+bv=0$, unique factorization implies $a\mid v$, and then $(u,v)$ is a multiple of $(b,-a)$. The column in step 2.1 is $\delta_{p,q}(b,-a)^T$. To show $\delta_{p,q}\in\Lambda$, replace signed exponents by $m=|p|$, $n=|q|$, which changes each factor only by a unit. Set $A=(t^m-1)/(t-1)$ and $B=(t^n-1)/(t-1)$. They are coprime; since $m,n$ divide $mn$, both divide $(t^{mn}-1)/(t-1)$. Unique factorization gives $AB\mid(t^{mn}-1)/(t-1)$, hence $\delta_{m,n}=((t^{mn}-1)/(t-1))/(AB)\in\Lambda$, and the signed quotient is a unit multiple. If $|p|=1$ or $|q|=1$, this quotient is a unit, so the same cyclic presentation gives $A_K=0$.

By [F5], $H_1$ of the cyclic cover of $P_{p,q}$ is $\ker d_1/\operatorname{im}d_2\cong\Lambda/(\delta_{p,q})$. The presentation complex and $E_K$ have the same fundamental group and the same homomorphism $\phi$; the fundamental groups of their cyclic covers are the corresponding kernels, and the deck action on their abelianizations is conjugation by a preimage of $1\in\mathbb Z$. Hurewicz therefore identifies their first-homology $\Lambda$-modules. Full AC [A1] supplies the countable-choice hypothesis of [F3] by [L1]; the deformation retraction then identifies the cyclic-cover homology of $E_K$ with that of $S^3\setminus K$. Thus $A_K\cong\Lambda/(\delta_{p,q})$.

The one-by-one presentation $[\delta_{p,q}]$ of $\Lambda/(\delta_{p,q})$ has $E_0$ generated by its sole $1\times1$ minor, namely $\delta_{p,q}$. Isomorphism invariance of the Alexander module and the definition [F6] give $E_0(A_K)=(\delta_{p,q})$ and hence $\Delta_K\doteq\delta_{p,q}$.
